title: Old age (Sn 4.6)
hookLine: read it: life is short; what is "mine" is lost at death
tomorrow: a monk leaves his vow. what does the next poem say he loses?

lines: NONE OF IT COMES WITH YOU.
CALLED OLD AGE. BARELY ABOUT IT.
cards: Some dreams are so real you wake up still reaching. The dog you had as a kid. A house you never lived in.
A friend you haven't talked to in years, laughing in your kitchen. Then the alarm goes, and none of it comes with you. Nothing from the dream is still yours.
The sixth poem of the chapter of eights uses that exact moment of waking. And here's the puzzle: the poem is called Old age, and it barely talks about getting old.

teach.h: LIFE IS SHORT. THEN IT TURNS.
teach.b: In paraphrase from the Sutta Nipata, it opens on age, briefly. Life is short. Even someone who lives long dies of old age in the end.
Then it turns. People grieve over what they call mine, because nothing they own lasts.
Whatever a person thinks, this is mine, that too is left behind at death. Then the dream. Just as someone who wakes up can't see what they met in sleep, you can't see the dear one who has died.
People we saw and heard, called by this name or that: only the name remains to be spoken.
And the last picture: the sage is like water on a lotus leaf, beading, rolling, not soaking in. So why call it Old age? Here's the solve.
Age takes things one at a time: strength, people, places, finally the body. What makes each loss tear instead of fall away is the label we glued on first.
Mine. The poem doesn't say stop loving. It says hold like a lotus leaf holds water: fully there, not stuck.

how: Buddhist teachers use the lotus as a picture of living in the world without being stained by it, and some lay Buddhists practice giving things away while alive as a way to loosen the sense of 'mine'.

o: a long life given as a reward for merit
growing old, and the 'mine' it takes away
the age when a monk may teach on his own

games.q: inside the poem — tap the pairs.
p: short, even for those who live long
like water on a lotus leaf

s: the poem called Old age is mostly about growing old
a few lines on age, then it turns to 'mine' and letting go.
the poem says that of someone who has died, only the name remains
people we saw and heard, called by this name or that: only the name remains to be spoken.
the poem says to stop loving people because they'll die
it warns about the grip of 'mine'; the sage holds like a lotus leaf holds water.

games.q: a friend borrows your sketchbook and loses it on the bus. you're crushed. by the poem, where's the sting coming from?
o: the 'mine' glued onto it, which was always going to be left behind.
the sketchbook itself; real things matter, and that's the end of it.
your friend; trust is broken and the poem says to guard what's yours.
games.why: the poem doesn't call the loss nothing. it says people grieve over what they've made 'mine', and points to the grip as the place the sting lives.

practice: Sit with your hands resting palms up on your knees, open, like two leaves. As thoughts of things you call mine arrive, a phone, a room, a plan, a person, let each one land on the open hands and roll off again.
Keep the palms open until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Old age: the poem's doorway. Life is short, and what we call mine is left behind; the sage holds things like water on a lotus leaf.

orig.note: Pali: old age, decay. The poem is the Jarā Sutta.

carryVoice: For the road: what's mine, less than it feels like and lighter for it. Poem six, read.

drop.name: the chapter of eights, read whole
